why this chapterThe answer depends on computing the vernier constant (least count) of a vernier callipers, VC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD, which is taught under Vernier Calliper and Least Count in Units and Measurements.
subtopic 1Vernier Calliper and Screw Gauge
subtopic 2not assigned (one subtopic chosen)
why this subtopicThe answer is the vernier constant VC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD = 0.1 mm/(N+1) = 1/(100(N+1)) cm, computed from the vernier callipers' scale relation, which is taught under Vernier Calliper and Screw Gauge.
printed in the booklet
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
In a vernier calipers, (N + 1) divisions of vernier scale coincide with N divisions of main scale. If 1 MSD represents 0.1 mm, the vernier constant (in cm) is:
  1. 110N
  2. 1100(N+1)
  3. 100N
  4. 10(N + 1)
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. Since (N+1) VSD = N MSD, 1 VSD = NN+1 MSD.
  2. VC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD = (1 - NN+1)MSD = 1N+1 MSD.
  3. 1 MSD = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm = 1100 cm.
  4. VC = 1100(N+1) cm, which is option 2.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
22 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsFrom (N+1) VSD = N MSD, write 1 VSD = N/(N+1) MSD → Vernier constant = 1 MSD - 1 VSD = MSD/(N+1) → Convert 1 MSD = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm and substitute to get the result in cm
confusing options2 of 4 · options 1, 2
Options 1 and 2 are both small fractions of the right form; option 1 is what a candidate reaches by dividing by N instead of N+1 and slipping the mm-to-cm conversion by a factor of ten, while options 3 and 4 grow with N and give a vernier constant of many cm, which is impossible.
why it is trickyMedium: three short, standard steps on a formula every candidate has drilled, and the options cut it to two on sight because 100N and 10(N+1) cm are absurd magnitudes for a least count; the remaining pair differs in both the N vs N+1 denominator and a power of ten, so careful work separates them cleanly.
the catchThe unit trap: MSD is given in mm but the answer is asked in cm, and the N vs N+1 denominator is easy to swap when (N+1) VSD coincide with N MSD rather than the usual N VSD with (N-1) MSD.

If the monochromatic source in Young’s double slit experiment is replaced by white light, then
  1. Interference pattern will disappear.
  2. There will be a central dark fringe surrounded by a few coloured fringes.
  3. There will be a central bright white fringe surrounded by a few coloured fringes.
  4. All bright fringes will be of equal width.
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. At the central point the path difference is Δ x = 0 for every wavelength λ.
  2. So every colour has a maximum there, and their overlap gives a central bright white fringe.
  3. Fringe width β = λ Dd differs for each λ, so away from the centre the maxima separate into a few coloured fringes, which is option 3.

A horizontal force 10 N is applied to a block A as shown in figure. The mass of blocks A and B are 2 kg and 3 kg respectively. The blocks slide over a frictionless surface. The force exerted by block A on block B is :
  1. Zero
  2. 4 N
  3. 6 N
  4. 10 N
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. Both blocks move together on the frictionless surface, so a = FmA + mB = 102+3 = 2 m/s2.
  2. The only horizontal force on B is the contact force from A: N = mB a.

stepsTreat A and B as one system on the frictionless floor: common acceleration a = F/(mA + mB) = 10/5 m/s2 → Isolate B: the only horizontal force on B is the contact force from A, so N = mB x a
confusing options2 of 4 · options 2, 3

printed in the booklet
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Choose the correct circuit which can achieve the bridge balance.
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · medium
  1. Arms: P = 10 Ω (top-left), Q = 10 Ω (top-right), R = 15 Ω (bottom-left), S = bottom-right arm containing 5 Ω and diode D.
  2. Balance condition: PQ = RS ⇒ 1010 = 15S ⇒ S = 15 Ω.
  3. So the bottom-right arm must conduct and have resistance 15 Ω: 5 + rD = 15 ⇒ rD = 10 Ω, i.e. a forward-biased diode in series with 5 Ω.
  4. In options 1, 2, 3 the long plate (positive) of E is on the left, so current flows left node → bottom node → right node in the lower arms; in option 4 the battery is reversed.
  5. Option 1: diode points from the bottom node toward the right node, so it is forward biased and in series with 5 Ω; balance is possible with rD = 10 Ω.
  6. Option 2: diode points the other way, so it is reverse biased; the arm is open and current flows through G via the 15 Ω arm, no balance.
  7. Option 4: diode as in option 1 but battery reversed, so it is reverse biased; no balance.
  8. Option 3: diode in parallel with 5 Ω gives S ≤ 5 Ω ≠ 15 Ω; no balance.
  9. Hence the answer is option 1.

The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Kc = [N2][O2][NO]2 = (3.0×10-3)(4.2×10-3)(2.8×10-3)2.
  2. Kc = 12.6×10-67.84×10-6 = 1.607.
  3. Starting with 0.1 M NO and degree of dissociation α: [NO] = 0.1(1-α), [N2] = [O2] = 0.05α.
  4. Kc = (0.05α)2(0.1(1-α))2 = (0.5α1-α)2 = 1.607.
  5. 0.5α1-α = 1.607 = 1.268.
  6. 0.5α = 1.268 - 1.268α ⇒ α = 1.2681.768 = 0.717, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
44 highagree
difficultyhard · 4 steps
stepsCompute Kc from the given equilibrium concentrations: Kc = [N2][O2]/[NO]2 = (3.0e-3)(4.2e-3)/(2.8e-3)2, about 1.6 → Set up the ICE table for 0.1 M NO: NO = 0.1(1 - α), N2 = O2 = 0.05 α (the factor of 1/2 from the 2:1 stoichiometry) → Write Kc = (0.05 α)2 / (0.1(1 - α))2 and take the square root of both sides: α / (2(1 - α)) = Kc, about 1.27 → Solve the linear equation for α, then match it against the options
confusing options2 of 4 · options 3, 4
Options 1, 2 and 3 are one number shifted by powers of ten, and 3 is the only member of that family with a sensible size for a Kc above 1, so a candidate who slips on the half-factor or the square root and lands near 0.9 will take 3; option 4 is the value the full working reaches.
why it is trickyHard: four steps that take a while to carry out. You divide powers of ten to get Kc, take the square root of a number that is not a perfect square, keep the 1/2 stoichiometric factor in the ICE table, and then solve for α. Dropping the factor of two or skipping the square root moves α a long way, and option 3 is a large-α rival waiting for that mistake.
the catchThe 2:1 stoichiometry makes N2 and O2 each 0.05 alpha, not 0.1 alpha, and the method only works if you notice the expression is a perfect square and take the root. Both are easy places to lose a factor under time pressure. Options 1 to 3 are a decimal-shift family, so the order of magnitude has to be right as well.

why it is trickyOnly two checks, but each statement is a near-copy of an NCERT line with one word carrying the verdict -- 'acidic' in II is the altered line, and 'a gene cry IAc' in I is a narrowing that a careful candidate may wrongly or rightly reject -- so three of the four options stay live and elimination does not help.
the catchAltered-line distractor: Statement II is NCERT's protoxin sentence with 'alkaline' changed to 'acidic', a single keyword a candidate reading for the familiar idea skips; Statement I's wording 'coded by a gene cry IAc' invites a second doubt that opens option 4.

solver reasoning: Bt toxins are coded by a family of cry genes (cryIAc is only one, specific to bollworms), so Statement I is false; the protoxin is activated by the alkaline, not acidic, pH of the insect gut, so Statement II is false.

  1. x10(kcal m-2) yr-1

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · medium
  1. Apply the 10% law: only about 10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next.
  2. Energy reaching the second trophic level = 0.1 × 100x = 10x (kcal m-2) yr-1.
  3. Energy reaching the third trophic level = 0.1 × 10x = x (kcal m-2) yr-1, which is option 2.

difficultyhard · 2 steps
stepsRecall Lindeman's 10 percent law: only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next. → Count the transfers from the first to the third trophic level (two, not three) and divide 100x by 10 twice.
confusing options3 of 4 · options 1, 2, 3
Option 3 is exactly what a candidate gets after applying the 10% cut once (thinking of level 2, or counting one transfer), option 1 is what they get after applying it three times (one cut per level named), and option 2 comes from the correct two transfers; option 4 is dead because the x cancels and leaves a pure number, which cannot be an energy flow that scales with x.
why it is trickyTwo short steps, but the options are built around an off-by-one count of transfers: 10x and x/10 sit on either side of the correct value, so the 10% law alone does not settle it and the candidate has to count transfers, not levels; the stem also says 'GPP of the third trophic level' while giving an NPP at the first, a mismatch of terms that can push a careless candidate into adding or dropping a step.
the catchOff-by-one trap: the third trophic level is two transfers from the first, and the distractors are exactly one transfer too few (10x) and one too many (x/10). The loose use of 'GPP' for a consumer level (GPP strictly belongs to producers) adds a terminology wobble that can make a candidate second-guess the setup.

solver reasoning: By Lindeman's 10% law, energy available to each next trophic level is 10% of the previous: 100x -> 10x (second) -> x (third).

confusing options2 of 4 · options 1, 2
Option 2 (B only) is live because statement B gives the right phenotype for every member and only the inheritance check (homozygous parents have no i to pass on) rules it out; options 3 and 4 include statements that put AB or A in the wrong slot and fall on sight.
why it is trickyMedium: two short steps of Mendelian recall, with options 3 and 4 eliminated by a slot-order glance, but one real rival remains -- B only is what a candidate gets by checking phenotypes alone, and only the ii-child-needs-heterozygous-parents step separates it from A only.
the catchStatement B is phenotypically correct for all three people, so a candidate who checks only phenotypes and forgets the child must receive i from both parents is drawn to option 2.

difficultymedium · 2 steps
stepsRecall that mitochondria and chloroplasts are both double-membrane-bound organelles, so Statement I is judged at once → Recall the NCERT line on membrane permeability (in the chloroplast it is the inner membrane that is described as relatively less permeable) and decide whether Statement II's mitochondria-versus-chloroplast comparison holds
confusing options2 of 4 · options 1, 3
Statement I is a textbook fact, so options 2 and 4 fall on sight; options 1 and 3 differ only on Statement II, an altered version of the NCERT 'inner membrane is relatively less permeable' line, which sounds familiar enough to accept and is odd enough to reject.
why it is trickyMedium: two short recalls, and Statement I settles half the options straight away, but options 1 and 3 remain real rivals that only exact recall of which organelle's inner membrane NCERT calls 'relatively less permeable' can separate.
the catchStatement II reuses the printed phrase 'relatively less permeable' from the chloroplast description but turns it into a comparison between organelles that NCERT never prints, so a candidate who recognises the phrase may accept the altered line.

solver reasoning: Both mitochondria and chloroplasts are double-membrane bound; the mitochondrial inner membrane (cristae, ETS, needs specific transporters) is relatively less permeable, so both statements are taken as correct.
